title: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography
summary: This sub-technique covers command and control traffic protected with a symmetric algorithm, where one secret key both encrypts the plaintext and decrypts the ciphertext. Common choices seen in the field include the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), the Data Encryption Standard (DES), triple DES (3DES), Blowfish and RC4. Because only a single key is required, the implementation is small and fast, which suits malware that must fit into limited code and work on modest hardware. The weakness sits in key management: when the key is hard coded in the sample or stored in a configuration file, an analyst who recovers it can decrypt previously captured traffic. On the network the payload is simply unreadable bytes, so defenders lean on the process that opens the socket, the reputation of the destination, the periodicity of the beacon, and the mismatch between the claimed protocol and the observed behaviour.

beginner.definition: Symmetric encryption uses one single key to lock and unlock a message. Both sides must hold the same key. It is fast and simple, so malware often relies on it. This sub-technique describes the Encrypted Channel parent when that shared key method is used.
beginner.whyItMatters: Fast encryption means a small malware program can hide its commands easily. The same key protects both directions, so the code stays simple. If that key leaks, however, all past traffic can be read. For defenders this means the key is valuable evidence. Finding it in a sample can turn unreadable traffic into clear proof.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a symmetric algorithm such as AES, RC4 or Blowfish.
A secret key is created, and both the malware and the server must know it.
The malware encrypts each command with that key before sending it out.
The server uses the same key to decrypt the message and read it.
Replies are encrypted again with that same key and sent back to the host.
If the key is stored in the sample, an analyst can decrypt captured traffic.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with one front door key. Every flatmate carries a copy of the same key. Any of them can lock and unlock the door. That is convenient, but if one copy is lost, the door is open to whoever finds it. Symmetric encryption works in the same way. The sender and the receiver share one secret key. If an analyst finds a copy of that key, every message becomes readable.
takeaways: Symmetric means one shared key is used to lock and to unlock.
A key stored inside a sample can be recovered and used to decrypt traffic.
When content is unreadable, watch the process and the destination instead.

objectives: Define symmetric encryption and name two common algorithms used in this context.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the Encrypted Channel parent.
Describe why a hard coded key is a weakness for the attacker.
Explain what defenders can still observe in a symmetrically encrypted session.
Describe how an analyst recovers a stored key and applies it to captured traffic.
